attacks.claim: The open-data export publishes ward, zip, birth_year, gender alongside ranking and created_at per poll, on a public CC-BY site. Combined with fine-grained timestamps and small ward/zip cells, this makes individual residents linkable and re-identifiable, and it discloses demographic attributes that were collected for a different purpose (jury-pool balance reports).
attacks.evidence: "one CSV per poll on data.ourtown.org with columns ward, zip, birth_year, gender, ranking, verified, created_at. resident_id is removed before export."

attacks.claim: Verified residents' address, zip, birth_year and gender were collected for jury-pool balance reporting, yet the plan repurposes them for poll exports and public CSVs without stated consent or purpose limitation.
attacks.evidence: "Verified residents already have address, zip, birth_year, gender (collected at optional verification for the jury-pool-style demographic balance reports)."

attacks.claim: Mass SMS to ~142,000 voters using a purchased county voter file repurposes government registration data for unsolicited marketing-style outreach. Voter files are typically restricted to election/government purposes and may not allow this use; no consent basis is given.
attacks.evidence: "Purchase the county voter registration file from the County Clerk ($400, includes mobile numbers where provided)."

attacks.claim: Unsolicited automated SMS to 142,000 people (plus 3 reminders) under the TCPA requires prior express written consent for autodialed/marketing texts; purchased voter-file numbers do not satisfy that. Opt-out via STOP alone does not cure the initial send. Statutory damages are per message, so exposure is potentially enormous.
attacks.evidence: "send an automated SMS to every registered voter in the city (~142,000) with a link to the first poll, then 3 automated reminders over 10 days." / "Reply STOP handled by Twilio's default opt-out."

attacks.claim: Voter-file data use is likely restricted by state law and the clerk's licence terms; the plan has no review of permitted use, and the data is being loaded into a third-party service (Twilio) without DPA or disclosure.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: any legal review, permitted-use check, or data processing agreement for the county voter file or Twilio.

attacks.claim: Anonymous responses are protected only by device fingerprint and per-IP rate limiting, which are trivially bypassed (fingerprint spoofing, IP rotation). Unverified responses are still published as tallies; the 'verified vs all' split does not stop a brigade from distorting the 'all' column that staff and press may cite.
attacks.evidence: "1 response per poll per device fingerprint" / "unverified responses over 3/min from one IP are queued for review."

attacks.claim: The plan claims results cannot be masqueraded, but ward is self-selected for unverified users, so per-ward IRV results can be trivially manipulated. Also, the 'verified' flag is never defined as to whether a verified resident's response can also be submitted anonymously, risking double counting.
attacks.evidence: "Unverified responses are accepted; ward is self-selected for unverified users"

attacks.claim: The central premise is contradicted by the artifact's own survey: only 9% wanted polls on upcoming items, yet the plan calls Ward Voice the roadmap centerpiece and sets success on volume. The 'staff lack a structured way to hear from residents' claim has no supporting data.
attacks.evidence: "Polls on upcoming items — 9%" vs "is the centerpiece of the FY27 roadmap."

attacks.claim: The product solves a problem residents rank low; the top two survey requests (vote records with reasons, neighborhood alerts) are absent from the build.
attacks.evidence: "See how my council member voted on each item, and their stated reason — 61%" ... ABSENT from Section 7 timeline.

attacks.claim: The 30%-new-users target and 6,000-response goal have no baseline or rationale; the SMS outreach is the only mechanism to hit them, which makes success dependent on the compliance-risky step.
attacks.evidence: "6,000 poll responses in the first 30 days." / "30% of responses from residents not previously active on OurTown."

attacks.claim: Published open data and emailed PDFs are irreversible once released, and staff cannot delete responses, so mistakenly published or abusive/personal data cannot be retracted. There is no takedown or correction path.
attacks.evidence: "Staff cannot edit or delete responses" / "Open-data export (weekly, public, CC-BY)"

attacks.claim: The Monday 07:00 staff email and weekly export have no failure alerting, retry, or time-zone spec, and a 142k-recipient SMS run has no throttling or failure handling mentioned.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: retry, alerting, and send-rate limits for the SMS pipeline and export job.

attacks.claim: Targeting 5k concurrent users and 142k SMS sends in the same launch week, with no load plan for the SMS-triggered traffic spike, risks outages on a self-hosted Django/Postgres stack with no capacity evidence.
attacks.evidence: "load test (target 5k concurrent)" / "send an automated SMS to every registered voter in the city (~142,000)"

attacks.claim: Twilio per-message cost for ~142k×4 messages (~570k) is not budgeted; only the $400 file cost is stated.
attacks.evidence: "Purchase the county voter registration file from the County Clerk ($400"

attacks.claim: Drag-to-rank is the primary interaction in the ranking UI; the plan only says 'drag or tap-to-rank' with an accessibility pass deferred to week 5 for a 1-week window.
attacks.evidence: "resident ranking UI (mobile-first, drag or tap-to-rank)" / "Week 5: accessibility pass"

attacks.claim: Scope and mission mismatch: the anonymous-first constraint is undermined by the plan's push to tie resident responses to verified demographic fields, and the SMS outreach contradicts the stated anonymous-first, verification-optional agreement by requiring phone-number-based targeting of the whole electorate.
attacks.evidence: "Agreed constraint: the product is anonymous-first — residents can participate without verifying identity, and verification is always optional."
